title: Nawab of Awadh
capsule: The Nawabs of Awadh (Oudh) governed the most prosperous subah of the declining Mughal empire from 1722, when Saadat Khan — an Iranian-born Mughal noble of Sayyid origin from Nishapur — received the governorship and made it hereditary; the dynasty adopted Shia Islam as its court tradition. Under Asaf ud-Daula (r. 1775–1797) Lucknow became a preeminent center of Urdu poetry, Kathak dance, and Indo-Persian architecture, while the East India Company extracted successive territorial cessions and subsidiary-alliance payments. The Company annexed Awadh outright in February 1856 on grounds of 'misrule' under Wajid Ali Shah, who was exiled to Calcutta; his consort Begum Hazrat Mahal led Lucknow's resistance in the 1857 uprising until British recapture in March 1858.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory of Awadh is well established from Company records, revenue surveys, and treaties; outer borders fluctuated as cessions were imposed and are documented with moderate precision.
